title: Battle of Bloody Ridge (1951): The Meatgrinder of the East
subtitle: August 18 – September 5, 1951

lines: August 1951. A nameless ridge north of Yanggu, deep in the mountains of eastern Korea.
After days and nights of shelling, not a single tree was left standing on its crest.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Yet the moment the guns fell silent, enemy machine guns opened up again from the bare earth.
Bunkers buried deep in the ridge had ridden out the entire bombardment.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: In the end, men had to crawl up the slopes with rifles and grenades.
For every bunker they destroyed, someone fell on that slope.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: For this one ridge alone, South Korean and UN casualties would climb past two thousand eight hundred.
An American military newspaper gave it a chilling name.
Bloody Ridge.
This is the story of a three-week battle fought in the shadow of the truce talks.
By the summer of 1951, the war had ground to a halt near the 38th Parallel.
On July 10th, truce talks finally opened at Kaesong, an old city near the front line.

callouts.text: JULY 10, 1951 · TRUCE TALKS OPEN AT KAESONG

lines: But while the negotiators haggled, the guns at the front never stopped.
Every yard of ground held was leverage at the table.
scenes.label: UN correspondents covering the Kaesong truce talks (1951)

lines: The UN's main line of resistance was called the Kansas Line.
In the rugged mountains north of Yanggu, the US 2nd Infantry Division held the line.
The problem was a ridge just to the north.
North Korean observers hidden on it were calling down accurate artillery fire on UN positions.

callouts.text: ENEMY OBSERVATION POSTS → ARTILLERY ON UN LINES

lines: Eighth Army commander General James Van Fleet ordered the ridge taken.
He wanted the enemy's eyes put out, and South Korean units seasoned in battle.
In late July, the US 38th Infantry had set up a patrol base on Hill 1179, Taeu-san, to the east.
But heavy monsoon rains washed out the roads, and the main attack was put off until mid-August.
The objective: three peaks on a ridge running east to west.
From west to east, Hills 983, 940, and 773.
Hill 983, the highest of the three, looked straight down on the UN lines to the south.
The ridge was knife-edge narrow, with sheer slopes falling away on both sides.
The North Koreans had studded the ridge with log bunkers buried under earth and rock.
US records say the largest could hold as many as sixty men.
scenes.label: Dramatization

callouts.text: US records: largest bunkers held up to 60 men

lines: Trenches linked bunker to bunker, and minefields covered the approaches.
When the shells came, they took cover; when the shelling lifted, the guns came back out.

visual.head: NKPA Ridge Defenses
visual.note: Summary of US Army histories · Reconstructed

lines: On August 18th, 1951, the ROK 36th Regiment of the 5th Division led the first assault.
It was a South Korean regiment attached to the US 2nd Division.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Before the assault, UN artillery pounded the ridge.
Several artillery battalions, heavy mortars, and tanks: every gun in range was brought to bear.
scenes.label: US 2nd Div Sherman firing on enemy ridge bunkers (May 1951)

lines: Days of shelling turned the green ridge into bare, pale earth.
But when the barrage lifted, the enemy guns came back to life underground.
As the attackers climbed, the defenders threw and rolled grenades down on their heads.
With every step upward, more grenades came tumbling down.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: After five days of repeated frontal assaults, the 36th Regiment finally stood on the ridge.
But a fierce counterattack threw them back off it.

callouts.text: ROK records: taken Aug 25 → lost Aug 26

lines: As casualties mounted, the exhausted men's morale began to crack.
On August 27th, some units of the 36th Regiment broke and fell back.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The panic spread to elements of the US 9th Infantry, sent up in support.
That same day, the 9th's 2nd Battalion struck at Hill 983, and it too was forced back.
The next day, the 3rd Battalion went for Hill 773, and was driven off by a night attack.
It was the attackers who were being worn down, one battalion at a time.
On August 30th, the 9th Infantry hit Hill 940, in the center, head-on.
They got within a few hundred yards of the crest before bunker machine guns stopped them again.
scenes.label: A soldier climbing a steep slope (1951)

lines: Company A was cut to half strength, and its commander, Lieutenant Dunn, was killed.
Lieutenant Morrow, the artillery observer beside him, took command on the spot.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: And so the ridge was soaked in the blood of both sides.
The military newspaper Stars and Stripes called it Bloody Ridge.
For security it never named the place, so the men fighting there didn't know it was them.
On August 28th, the new X Corps commander, General Clovis Byers, changed the plan.
Instead of hammering one ridge, the whole corps front would push forward at once, starting August 31st.
The ROK 5th and 1st Marine Divisions drove on the Punchbowl; the ROK 7th, west of the ridge.
The enemy could no longer mass his guns and reserves in one place.
On August 31st, the Marines met little resistance and reached the Punchbowl's northern rim.
The flank of the North Koreans on the ridge was slowly being laid bare.
scenes.label: 1st Marine Division men resting near the Punchbowl (1951)

lines: Meanwhile, the 1st Battalion, 9th Infantry, broke the bunkers on Hill 773 one by one.
One platoon leader, his radio dead, took a bunker with nothing but grenades.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On September 3rd, after napalm and bombs swept the ridge, the attack went in again.
Company C, about eighty-five men strong, came out of it with about thirty.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Then the US 23rd and 38th Infantry swung wide around both ends of the ridge.
With the 9th still pressing the front, it was a double envelopment closing from three sides.
On September 4th and 5th, the 2nd Division finally reached the top of the ridge.
But the crest was strangely quiet.
The North Koreans had already slipped away to the north.
Left behind on the ridge were abandoned supplies and more than five hundred enemy dead, lying where they fell.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Per the US Army official history, South Korean and UN casualties topped 2,800.
By Korean records, the ROK 36th Regiment alone lost more than a thousand men.
The 2nd Division estimated enemy losses at over fifteen thousand.

visual.note: US Army history · ROK records (enemy: 2nd Div estimate)

lines: Why did one ridge cost so much blood?
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, the underground fortress.
The bunkers were heavy timbers piled with layer upon layer of earth and stone.
Unless a heavy shell landed squarely on top, they would not collapse.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Second, the limits of firepower.
The UN owned the sky and the artillery.
The 155-millimeter Long Tom was the best bunker-buster, but there were few of them.
Digging the enemy out of his bunkers was, in the end, a job for the infantry.
Third, the price of the frontal assault.
On a ridge that narrow, there was no room to spread out.
Men climbing in single file walked straight into the bunkers' fire.
Some platoons went into the attack made up mostly of replacements who had only just arrived.
scenes.label: Troops advancing uphill through smoke (1951)

lines: Fourth, the double envelopment.
In the end, the ridge was opened not from the front, but from the flanks.
Squeezed along the whole front and from both flanks, the enemy gave it up himself.
But the North Koreans had fallen back only a few miles, to fortified positions on another ridge to the north.
And on September 13th, the 2nd Division went on the attack again, toward that ridge.

callouts.text: SEP 13, 1951 · ON TO THE NEXT RIDGE

lines: That place would come to be called Heartbreak Ridge.
Bloody Ridge was only the beginning of a longer, harsher war for the hills.
Today, a memorial to the Battle of Bloody Ridge stands in Worun-ri, Yanggu County.
On those slopes, the search for those who never came home has gone on for years.
scenes.label: Bloody Ridge battle memorial · Yanggu (2009)

lines: A single line on the negotiating table cost thousands of lives on this ridge.
The ground they held is today's Yanggu, just south of the armistice line that still divides Korea.
A nameless ridge north of Yanggu.
To this day, its name remains Bloody Ridge.
